C0.quote: deciding whether there is a tie in a given approval-based multiwinner election

C1.quote: For most cases, our problems are computationally hard
C1.note: Complexity results (Sections 3-4) dominate. Simulations use the resampling and interval models. The empirical part uses PabuLib real data.

C2.1.quote: vi ’s approval set or vi ’s vote, interchangeably

C2.2.quote: each voter vi has a set A(vi ) ⊆ C of candidates

C2.3.quote: a group of voters expresses their preferences about a set of candidates
C2.3.note: The paper says voters express preferences, and in the interval model voter positions on [0,1] generate the approvals; both are attitudes not defined as the submitted input.

C2.4.quote: each voter indicates which of them he or she approves
C2.4.note: Approval sets are presented as what voters approve and are fed directly to the rule, with no statement about reporting or sincerity; ONE is excluded because C2.3 = Y.

C3.2.loc: Introduction, Section 2 Preliminaries, Section 5, Section 6 Summary

C4.1.note: No utility, welfare or satisfaction notions are used for voters. 'Satisfaction approval voting' is only a rule name.

C4.2.note: The term 'dichotomous preferences' is not used.

C5.1.note: Results concern ties, complexity and tie frequency. Proportionality is mentioned only descriptively in the introduction.

VOT.quote_behav: each voter vi has a set A(vi ) ⊆ C of candidates
VOT.note: Voters cast approval votes that are exogenous or generated by statistical cultures; this is a fixed action.

ORG.note: The organizer applies a prespecified rule and makes no choice in the model.

C9.2.quote: while this makes our data less realistic
C9.2.note: The claim that ties are a realistic possibility in real elections needs the assumption that the generated data represent real moderately sized elections. This is only partly stated: the resampling ϕ is said to resemble real data, but PabuLib is conceded to be less realistic and no realism claim is made for the interval model.

C2.3.reason: The paper attributes preferences that voters 'express' and spatial positions that generate approvals, so a held attitude is referred to and C2.3 = Y.

C2.4.reason: A held attitude is present, which rules out ONE, and the approval set is described as what voters approve and is used directly with no submission statement.

C3.2.reason: C2.4 is IDU rather than ONE and C3.1 = NONE, so NA does not apply, and no sincerity statement is found.

C6.VOT.reason: The codebook counts fixed actions, and voters cast votes in the model, so they are present and non-strategic by implication.

C9.2.reason: The real-world tie-frequency claim relies on the data being representative, which the paper states only partly and partly hedges against.
